# Isleta 2.1.0
The island now says what your power just did — "Charging" or "On Battery" beside the battery, the same way it names the key you pressed for volume and brightness.
## New
- **Plugging in and unplugging say so in words.** The island widens beside the notch and shows "Charging" or "On Battery" next to the battery glyph, with the level beside it, then goes away on its own. A battery symbol with a small bolt in it and one without are hard to tell apart in a notch; the word is not. - **The same for the other power moments.** "Charged", "Low Battery", and "Low Power On" or "Low Power Off" when macOS switches the mode.
## Improved
- **Power keeps the readable half of the island when music is playing.** The word sits where the album cover would go and the track's own sliver moves to the other side, rather than the charger showing up as a bar with nothing to say what it measures.
## Requirements
macOS 26 or later, on Apple Silicon. Displays with a real notch get the island; a Mac without one gets a floating island on the main display.
## Known limitations
- **You cannot see who is calling.** macOS does not let apps outside Apple read that, or answer for you. Isleta shows that a call is happening and nothing more. - **Weather needs your location, or a city you type.** Isleta asks for neither until you use it. - **A connected device's battery is read once, when it connects.** It does not tick down as you wear them, and most non-Apple headphones report no level at all. - **A timer started by Siri, Shortcuts or Control Center can take a few seconds to appear.** One started by hand in Clock is there immediately. - **Replacing the system HUDs is off until you turn it on, and it needs Accessibility.** Quitting Isleta hands your keys straight back; if Isleta is force-quit, the system HUD stays out of the way until Isleta next starts. Brightness covers the built-in display only. - **The island sits above Mission Control.** In a real notch it covers nothing; a floating island can sit over the middle of the space labels. - **Today and tomorrow show five entries and then a count.** A busy pair of days says how many it could not fit rather than scrolling.

# Isleta 2.0.1
Turning a page is smoother, the day view holds its size, and a day with nothing on it now says so instead of looking empty by accident.
## Improved
- **Turning a page is smoother.** The three pages no longer redraw themselves on every frame of the swipe, so a day full of events or a playing track no longer makes the carousel stutter on its way past.
## Fixed
- **The day view's bottom edge stopped jumping up.** Opening today and tomorrow from the date, then changing track — or anything else arriving on the island — pulled the bottom edge up and cut the last row off. It now stays where it opened, whatever else happens. - **A day with no events says so.** "No events today" and "No events tomorrow", each in its own place, instead of a column that simply started at Tomorrow or stopped early. A free day and a day whose events failed to load looked identical before this.
## Requirements
macOS 26 or later, on Apple Silicon. Displays with a real notch get the island; a Mac without one gets a floating island on the main display.
## Known limitations

Isleta shows that a call is happening and nothing more. - **Weather needs your location, or a city you type.** Isleta asks for neither until you use it. - **A connected device's battery is read once, when it connects.** It does not tick down as you wear them, and most non-Apple headphones report no level at all. - **A timer started by Siri, Shortcuts or Control Center can take a few seconds to appear.** One started by hand in Clock is there immediately. - **Replacing the system HUDs is off until you turn it on, and it needs Accessibility.** Quitting Isleta hands your keys straight back; if Isleta is force-quit, the system HUD stays out of the way until Isleta next starts. # Isleta 2.0.0
The notch became something you can browse. Three pages — your day, your music, the weather — turned with a two-finger swipe, with everything that arrives on its own taking the stage in front of them. Now in German, French and Spanish.
## New
- **Three pages, and a swipe between them.** Today, Music and Weather. Swipe two fingers across an open island to turn the page. They wrap, so there is no end to walk into. - **Your day, in the notch.** What is next in your calendar, with a button that joins the meeting. Choose which calendars count in Settings. - **The weather where you are.** Today's high and low, what it feels like, and the chance of rain for the next few days. Use your location, or type a city and pick it from the list. - **When it's raining, it rains in the island.** The drops land on its bottom edge. Snow falls too, and both stop if you have asked macOS to reduce motion. - **A music page that shows the whole track.** Long titles scroll and then settle, the album artwork lends the island its color, and the audio format shows as a small badge. - **Up Next.** The queue your player is working through, the output device, favorite and playback speed. Double-click anything in the list to play it. - **Drop files on the island to convert them.** Images, images to PDF, video, audio, Word, RTF, HTML, spreadsheets and presentations. Search the shelf, preview with Space, and look back through everything Isleta has made for you. - **Drop audio or video to transcribe it.** The text lands beside the original. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is asked of you. - **Copy Link** puts a shareable iCloud link on your clipboard. For files outside iCloud Drive it offers AirDrop instead. - **Isleta can answer your volume and brightness keys.** Turn it on under Sources and the island replaces macOS's own HUD rather than sitting beside it. Volume and brightness are separate switches, both off until you turn them on. - **A card on the lock screen** showing what is playing. It arrives when the Mac locks and leaves the moment you unlock it. Off until you turn it on. - **AirPods and other Bluetooth devices announce themselves** when they connect, with the battery level if the device reports one. - **Battery, calls and timers.** The charger going in and out, a low battery, Low Power Mode, a call in progress with how long it has been going, and timers you start in Clock. - **A first run that asks once.** Eight short screens, five of them permissions — accessibility, music, calendar, weather and devices — each showing what the permission is for, and which button to press, before it asks. Skip any of them and the rest of Isleta still works. - **A list of apps the island stays out of entirely**, for full-screen video or a presentation. - **Keyboard shortcuts** for opening the island and showing your day, under General. Opening the island ships bound to ⌃⌥⌘I, because Isleta has no Dock icon and its menu bar item can be hidden; showing your day is unassigned until you assign it. - **Quick actions in the menu bar** for whatever is on the island right now. The icon can be hidden; Quit and Open Setup Guide live in About as well. - **German, French and Spanish**, following your Mac's language.
## Improved
- **Settings is a much smaller place.** Four panes instead of seven, and roughly a third as many controls. What went were the settings asking you a question Isleta can answer for itself. - **The island is black in a real notch and glass where it floats**, and no longer asks you to choose. It was never a matter of taste, so it is no longer a setting. - **The whole island moves as one.** Its width, height and corners travel together, so opening it reads as a single motion rather than two. - **Reduce motion, reduce transparency and increase contrast are honored throughout.**
## Fixed
- **Settings opens on the desktop you are looking at**, rather than the one you last opened it on. Opening Settings now closes the island. - **Playing music costs a fraction of what it did.** A playing track is now about as light as a quiet island. - **Closing Up Next gives the island its height back.** The ✕ used to leave it tall. - **AirPods connecting no longer hangs Isleta at launch.**
## Requirements
macOS 26 or later, on Apple Silicon. Displays with a real notch get the island; a Mac without one gets a floating island on the main display.
